posts.title: Autumn Landscape Pastel Painting | Ian Risley
posts.description: SEPTEBER 2016 Autumn can be a wonderful time to get outdoors with your sketchbook or painting materials, looking for the changing colours and light that make the season so distinctive. Artist Ian Risley shares a soft pastel painting inspired by an afternoon at Bradgate Park in Leicestershire. Using a limited selection of colours, he builds up the landscape with layers, blending and careful highlights to capture the warmth of the afternoon sunshine and the first hints of autumn. posts.title: Ink Drawing Techniques: Using Line Weight for Depth | John Harrison
posts.description: Click images to enlarge A confident ink drawing can be wonderfully effective, but using the same thickness of line throughout can sometimes leave a sketch looking a little flat. One simple way to introduce depth and make your subject easier to read is to vary the weight of your lines, using thicker marks to emphasise selected areas and bring different elements forward. Artist John Harrison explains how he uses this technique in his architectural sketches and pen and wash drawings, sharing practical examples to help you make more of your own linework. I love a good ink drawing: and the majority of my work — whether in a sketchbook or at a workshop or demonstration — starts off with a black drawing, done in ink. This initial drawing is almost always created using a fine nib size, usually a 0.1 Micron or Unipin . posts.title: Experimental Watercolour Techniques: Teasel Wood | Jane Betteridge
posts.description: From Paint & Create November 2017, the magazine of the SAA Click images to enlarge Watercolour doesn’t always have to behave as expected! By combining traditional painting techniques with a few unexpected materials, you can create fascinating textures and effects that would be difficult to achieve with a brush alone. In this demonstration, Jane Betteridge explores a playful approach to painting a winter woodland, using wet-in-wet washes, cling film, modelling paste and bronze powder to bring her silver birch trees and teasels to life. Along the way, she shares useful advice on colour choices and how to make the most of those happy surprises. I love watching wet-in-wet watercolour washes mixing and merging on the paper rather than in the palette.
